title: Guardrail placement: input, retrieval, output, tool
summary: A guard only sees what passes through its position. Input, retrieved content, tool calls and output each carry different risks, so placement decides what a guard can catch and what it costs in latency.
useIf: You are deciding where to put checks around a RAG or agent request and how much latency each may add.
avoidIf: You treat guardrails as one filter on the final answer: that misses untrusted documents, tool side effects and early leaks.

explain.md: Foundry guardrails define four **intervention points**: user input, tool call (preview, agents only), tool response (preview, agents only) and output [[r1]]. NeMo Guardrails names five rail types: input, retrieval, dialog, execution and output, where retrieval rails filter chunks and execution rails check tool calls [[r13]]. Different names, same idea: each point sees different data.

**Input guards** catch attacks and unwanted topics before the model spends tokens. **Retrieval guards** treat retrieved chunks as untrusted: a document can carry an instruction that the user never typed, which Prompt Shields calls a document (indirect) attack [[r3]]. **Tool guards** run before a side effect happens, so they must sit in front of execution, not behind the answer. **Output guards** check what the user will see. Microsoft's defence-in-depth guidance combines prompt hardening, Spotlighting, Prompt Shields and deterministic blocking of exfiltration paths, not one filter [[r11]].

**Latency.** No vendor in the sources publishes guard latency, so measure it. As an author estimate, a classifier call adds tens to a few hundred milliseconds, and an LLM judge adds a full model call of one to several seconds. Sequential guards add up. Independent guards run in parallel add only the slowest. Streaming changes the output trade-off: the default buffers and filters chunks, while the asynchronous filter streams token by token and guarantees the stop signal only within about 1,000 characters [[r9]].

explain.title: Where each guard stands in a RAG request
explain.alt: A user prompt passes an input guard, retrieval runs, a chunk guard checks retrieved content, the model runs, then a tool guard checks proposed tool calls and an output guard checks the answer before it reaches the user.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  U[User] --> G1[Input guard]
  G1 --> R[Retrieve]
  R --> G2[Chunk guard]
  G2 --> M[Model]
  M --> G3[Tool guard]
  M --> G4[Output guard]
  G4 --> A[Answer]

explain.title: Retrieval can fail open
explain.md: Retrieve calls without a user identity header return unfiltered results from indexed sources [[tr2]]. A guard placed after retrieval cannot restore a permission check that was skipped before it.

use: Put an input guard in front of every model call that accepts user text
Put a chunk guard on retrieved or tool-returned content when sources are not fully trusted
Put a tool guard before any call with a side effect
Put an output guard where harm comes from what the user reads
avoid: Avoid a single output-only guard for agents: tool side effects happen before the answer
Avoid running every guard sequentially when they are independent
Avoid assuming the model-level guardrail covers tool calls on an agent
flips: Latency budget is tight: run input guards in parallel with retrieval and reserve LLM judges for high-risk routes
Sources are fully trusted and curated: the chunk guard can be lighter or sampled
Tools are read-only: tool-call guards matter less, tool-response scanning matters more

pitfalls.symptom: An agent sends a harmful email although the final answer passed the output guard
pitfalls.cause: No guard stood in front of the tool call
pitfalls.fix: Add tool-call controls or a deterministic allow list before execution

pitfalls.symptom: Added guards double the response time
pitfalls.cause: Independent checks were chained in sequence
pitfalls.fix: Run independent guards in parallel and tier the expensive ones

pitfalls.symptom: A planted instruction in a PDF steers the answer
pitfalls.cause: Only user input was scanned, not retrieved chunks
pitfalls.fix: Scan chunks and tool responses for document attacks and reduce tool privileges

pitfalls.symptom: Tool calls are unscanned after an agent guardrail was created
pitfalls.cause: An agent's guardrail fully overrides its model's, and it had no tool controls
pitfalls.fix: Include tool call and tool response controls in the agent guardrail

scenarios.title: Read-only assistant over uploaded documents
scenarios.situation: Users upload PDFs and ask questions. The assistant has no tools and answers in under three seconds. Uploaded files come from outside the company.
constraints: Moderate harm if the answer is steered
unknowns: Can the answer reach other users?
scenarios.question: Which guards do you place?

options.name: Input guard in parallel with retrieval, a chunk guard for document attacks, and an output guard
options.why: The risk sits in the documents, so chunk scanning is essential, and parallel input checks protect the budget.
options.tradeoff: More guard calls and a small false positive rate on benign text.

options.name: Output guard only
options.tradeoff: A steered but plausible answer passes, and the cost of generation is already spent.

options.name: Input guard only
options.why: The user prompt is clean while the attack lives in the document.
options.tradeoff: Right for chat with no retrieval and no documents.

flips.if: Documents come only from a curated, trusted library
flips.then: Sample chunk scanning and keep input and output guards.

flips.if: Latency budget shrinks below one second
flips.then: Keep only deterministic checks inline and move model-based guards to async review.

scenarios.takeaway: Guard the place where the untrusted content enters, not only the place where the user types.

scenarios.title: Agent that can send email
scenarios.situation: An agent reads a mailbox through a tool and can send replies. It streams answers. A mistaken or injected send cannot be undone.
unknowns: Is human approval available for sends?
scenarios.question: Where must the strongest guard stand?

options.name: Before the send: tool-call guard plus a deterministic allow list and approval, with tool-response scanning on the mailbox read
options.why: The harm happens at execution, so the check has to stand in front of it, and mailbox text is an indirect attack path.
options.tradeoff: Tool-call and tool-response controls are preview, and approvals add friction.

options.name: Input and output guards, plus human review of sent mail afterwards
options.why: Catches obvious problems and gives an audit trail.
options.tradeoff: Review happens after an irreversible send.

options.name: Output guard only
options.why: The email is already sent when the final answer is checked.
options.tradeoff: Right for text-only assistants with no side effects.

flips.then: Output and audit guards are enough.
Use deterministic allow lists and approvals in your own code.

scenarios.takeaway: Put the strongest guard in front of the action that cannot be undone.

quiz.q: An agent's final answers pass the output guard, yet it sent a bad email. What is the most likely gap?
options: The embedding model was too small
No guard stood in front of the tool call
quiz.explain: Side effects occur before the answer is produced, so a tool-call guard or deterministic control must stand in front of execution. Embedding size, reranking and staleness do not explain a bad send.

quiz.q: Which are valid ways to protect a tight latency budget?
options: Run independent input guards in parallel with retrieval
Reserve LLM judges for high-risk routes
Use deterministic checks inline for the cheapest filters
quiz.explain: Parallelism, tiering and cheap deterministic checks save time. Sequential chains add the sum of their latencies.

quiz.q: Match each NeMo Guardrails rail type to its job.

pairs.r: Checks the user message before the model

quiz.explain: Each rail type sees a different part of the request. NeMo also has a dialog rail type that governs conversation flow.

flashcards.front: Name the four Foundry guardrail intervention points.
flashcards.back: User input, tool call (preview, agents only), tool response (preview, agents only) and output.

flashcards.front: Why scan retrieved chunks and tool responses?
flashcards.back: They are untrusted text that can carry instructions the user never typed, so input guards alone miss document attacks.

flashcards.front: How do parallel guards affect latency?
flashcards.back: Independent parallel guards add roughly the slowest one. Sequential guards add the sum.
